\[
\frac{x^{2}}{20}-\frac{y^{2}}{24}=1\qquad\Bigl(a^{2}=20,\;b^{2}=24\Bigr),
\]
so a convenient parametrisation is  

\[
(x,y)=\bigl(a\sec\theta,\;b\tan\theta\bigr),\qquad 
a=2\sqrt5,\;b=2\sqrt6 .
\]

---

### 1.  Geometry of the rhombus  

If the four vertices \(A,B,C,D\) lie on the hyperbola and the diagonals meet at the origin,
the opposite vertices are opposite vectors:

\[
C=-A,\qquad D=-B .
\]

Hence the rhombus is the parallelogram with vertices  

\[
A=\mathbf a,\;B=\mathbf b,\;C=-\mathbf a,\;D=-\mathbf b .
\]

For a parallelogram centred at the origin to be a **rhombus** the four sides must have equal
lengths.  The side lengths are  

\[
|A\!-\!B|=|\mathbf a-\mathbf b|,\qquad 
|B\!-\!C|=|\mathbf b+\mathbf a| .
\]

Equality of these two lengths gives  

\[
|\mathbf a-\mathbf b|^{2}=|\mathbf a+\mathbf b|^{2}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\mathbf a\!\cdot\!\mathbf b=0 .
\]

Thus the two position vectors \(\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf b\) must be **orthogonal**.

---

### 2.  Orthogonal points on the hyperbola  

Write  

\[
\mathbf a=(a\sec\phi,\;b\tan\phi),\qquad 
\mathbf b=(a\sec\theta,\;b\tan\theta)
\]

with parameters \(\phi,\theta\).  
The orthogonality condition \(\mathbf a\!\cdot\!\mathbf b=0\) becomes  

\[
a^{2}\sec\phi\sec\theta+b^{2}\tan\phi\tan\theta=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
20\sec\phi\sec\theta+24\tan\phi\tan\theta=0 .
\]

Using \(\sec\alpha=1/\cos\alpha\) and \(\tan\alpha=\sin\alpha/\cos\alpha\),

\[
20+24\sin\phi\sin\theta=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\sin\phi\sin\theta=-\frac{5}{6}.
\tag{1}
\]

For a given \(\theta\) we can always choose \(\phi\) satisfying (1) provided  

\[
\bigl|\sin\theta\bigr|\ge\frac{5}{6},
\]

because then \(\sin\phi=-\dfrac{5}{6\sin\theta}\) lies in \([-1,1]\).

Thus the admissible points \(B\) correspond to parameters \(\theta\) with  

\[
|\sin\theta|>\frac{5}{6}
\quad(\text{the equality case would give }\cos\phi=0,
\text{ i.e. a point at infinity, which is not allowed}).
\]

---

### 3.  Length of diagonal \(BD\)

The diagonal \(BD\) joins \(\mathbf b\) and \(-\mathbf b\); its length is  

\[
BD=2\|\mathbf b\|\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
BD^{2}=4\bigl(x^{2}+y^{2}\bigr).
\]

For \(\mathbf b=(a\sec\theta,\;b\tan\theta)\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
x^{2}+y^{2}&=a^{2}\sec^{2}\theta+b^{2}\tan^{2}\theta\\
&=20\sec^{2}\theta+24\tan^{2}\theta\\
&=20\bigl(1+\tan^{2}\theta\bigr)+24\tan^{2}\theta\\
&=20+44\tan^{2}\theta .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
BD^{2}=4\bigl(20+44\tan^{2}\theta\bigr)=80+176\tan^{2}\theta .
\tag{2}
\]

Write \(u=\sin^{2}\theta\;(0<u<1)\).  Since \(\tan^{2}\theta=\dfrac{\sin^{2}\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta}
=\dfrac{u}{1-u}\), (2) becomes  

\[
BD^{2}=80+176\frac{u}{1-u}.
\tag{3}
\]

The orthogonality condition forces \(|\sin\theta|\ge\frac56\), i.e.  

\[
u\ge\frac{25}{36}.
\]

Because the function \(\displaystyle f(u)=80+176\frac{u}{1-u}\) is strictly increasing for
\(0<u<1\), the smallest possible value of \(BD^{2}\) occurs as \(u\) approaches the
lower bound \(25/36\) from above.  Substituting \(u=\frac{25}{36}\) into (3) gives the
limit

\[
\lim_{u\downarrow 25/36}BD^{2}=80+176\frac{\frac{25}{36}}{1-\frac{25}{36}}
=80+176\frac{25}{11}=80+400=480 .
\]

The bound \(u=25/36\) would require \(\sin\phi=-1\) (so \(\phi=-\pi/2\)), which makes
\(\sec\phi\) undefined; consequently the value \(BD^{2}=480\) is **not attained**, but
\(BD^{2}\) can be made arbitrarily close to it from above.

Thus every admissible rhombus satisfies  

\[
BD^{2}>480,
\]

and \(480\) is the greatest real number that is less than \(BD^{2}\) for **all** such
rhombi (the greatest lower bound, i.e. the infimum).

\boxed{480}
\]

\[

### 1.  Using the right‑angle condition  

The condition \(\overline{IA}\perp\overline{OI}\) means that in the
right triangle \(AIO\)

\[
\angle AIO=90^{\circ},\qquad AO=R .
\]

Hence, by the Pythagorean theorem  

\[
R^{2}=AI^{2}+OI^{2}.
\tag{1}
\]

Now  

\[
AI=\frac{r}{\sin\frac A2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad 
OI^{2}=R(R-2r)
\]

(the latter is the well‑known Euler formula \(OI^{2}=R(R-2r)\)).
Substituting \(R=13,\;r=6\) into (1) gives  

\[
169=\frac{36}{\sin^{2}\frac A2}+13 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\sin^{2}\frac A2=\frac{36}{156}=\frac{3}{13},
\qquad
\sin\frac A2=\sqrt{\frac{3}{13}},\qquad
\cos\frac A2=\sqrt{\frac{10}{13}} .
\tag{2}
\]

From (2)

\[
\sin A =2\sin\frac A2\cos\frac A2
       =\frac{2\sqrt{30}}{13},
\qquad
\cos A =\cos^{2}\frac A2-\sin^{2}\frac A2
       =\frac{7}{13},
\qquad
a=BC=2R\sin A =4\sqrt{30}. \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The angle between \(AI\) and \(AO\)

In \(\triangle AIO\) the acute angle at \(A\) is  

\[
\alpha=\angle IAO .
\]

Because the triangle is right at \(I\),

\[
\tan\alpha=\frac{OI}{AI}
          =\frac{\sqrt{R(R-2r)}}{\,r/\sin\frac A2\,}
          =\frac{\sqrt{13}}{\,6/\sqrt{3/13}\,}
          =\frac{1}{2\sqrt3}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\sin\alpha=\frac1{\sqrt{13}},\qquad
\cos\alpha=\frac{2\sqrt3}{\sqrt{13}} .
\tag{4}
\]

Geometrically one finds (for an acute triangle with \(B>C\))

\[
\alpha =\frac A2 + B -\frac{\pi}{2},
\qquad
\Longrightarrow\qquad
B=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac A2+\alpha ,
\]
and consequently  

\[
C=\pi-A-B=\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac A2-\alpha .
\]

Thus  

\[
B-C=2\alpha .
\tag{5}
\]

From (4) we obtain  

\[
\cos(B-C)=\cos(2\alpha)=2\cos^{2}\alpha-1
          =\frac{11}{13}. \tag{6}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Computing \(AB\cdot AC\)

Using the law of sines,
\[
b=CA=2R\sin B,\qquad c=AB=2R\sin C .
\]

Hence  

\[
bc =4R^{2}\sin B\sin C .
\]

With \(\sin B\sin C=\dfrac{\cos(B-C)+\cos A}{2}\) we obtain  

\[
bc =4R^{2}\Bigl(\frac{\cos(B-C)+\cos A}{2}\Bigr)
    =2R^{2}\bigl(\cos(B-C)+\cos A\bigr).
\]

Insert \(R=13\), \(\cos A=7/13\) and \(\cos(B-C)=11/13\) from (6):

\[
bc =2\cdot13^{2}\Bigl(\frac{11}{13}+\frac{7}{13}\Bigr)
    =2\cdot169\cdot\frac{18}{13}
    =338\cdot\frac{18}{13}
    =338\cdot\frac{18}{13}=338\cdot\frac{18}{13}=468 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{AB\cdot AC = 468}.
\]

### 1.  Use the distance \(OI\)

For any triangle  

\[
OI^{2}=R\bigl(R-2r\bigr).
\]

Hence  

\[
OI^{2}=13\bigl(13-12\bigr)=13\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad OI=\sqrt{13}.
\]

Since \(IA\perp OI\),

\[
OA^{2}=OI^{2}+IA^{2}\;\Longrightarrow\;13^{2}=13+IA^{2},
\]
so  

\[
IA^{2}=169-13=156\quad\Longrightarrow\quad IA=2\sqrt{39}.
\]

---

### 2.  Express \(IA\) in terms of \(\angle A\)

For the incenter \(I\),

\[
IA=\frac{r}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\frac{6}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}=2\sqrt{39}\;\Longrightarrow\;
\sin\frac{A}{2}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{39}}=\frac{\sqrt{39}}{13}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\cos\frac{A}{2}=\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}\frac{A}{2}}
               =\sqrt{1-\frac{39}{169}}=\frac{\sqrt{130}}{13}.
\]

Now  

\[
\sin A=2\sin\frac{A}{2}\cos\frac{A}{2}
      =2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{39}}{13}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{130}}{13}
      =\frac{2\sqrt{30}}{13},
\qquad 
\cos A=\cos^{2}\frac{A}{2}-\sin^{2}\frac{A}{2}
      =\frac{130-39}{169}=\frac{91}{169}.
\]

---

### 3.  Side \(a=BC\)

By the law of sines  

\[
a=2R\sin A=2\cdot13\cdot\frac{2\sqrt{30}}{13}=4\sqrt{30}.
\]

---

### 4.  Relate \(b=CA,\;c=AB\)

Let  

\[
b+c=S,\qquad bc=P.
\]

The area can be written in two ways:

\[
\Delta = rs = 6\cdot\frac{a+S}{2}=3\bigl(a+S\bigr),
\]
\[
\Delta =\frac{abc}{4R}= \frac{aP}{4R}= \frac{4\sqrt{30}\,P}{52}
        =\frac{\sqrt{30}\,P}{13}.
\]

Equating the two expressions for \(\Delta\),

\[
\frac{\sqrt{30}\,P}{13}=3\bigl(4\sqrt{30}+S\bigr)
\;\Longrightarrow\;
P=156+\frac{39}{\sqrt{30}}\,S. \tag{1}
\]

The law of cosines at vertex \(A\) gives  

\[
a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\cos A.
\]

Since \(b^{2}+c^{2}=S^{2}-2P\),

\[
a^{2}=S^{2}-2P\bigl(1+\cos A\bigr). \tag{2}
\]

We have  

\[
a^{2}= (4\sqrt{30})^{2}=480,\qquad 
\cos A=\frac{91}{169},\qquad 
1+\cos A=\frac{260}{169}=\frac{20}{13}.
\]

Substituting these into (2),

\[
S^{2}=480+\frac{40}{13}P. \tag{3}
\]

---

### 5.  Solve for \(S\) and \(P\)

Insert \(P\) from (1) into (3):

\[
S^{2}=480+\frac{40}{13}\Bigl(156+\frac{39}{\sqrt{30}}S\Bigr)
     =480+480+4\sqrt{30}\,S,
\]
\[
S^{2}-4\sqrt{30}\,S-960=0.
\]

Hence  

\[
S=\frac{4\sqrt{30}\pm\sqrt{(4\sqrt{30})^{2}+4\cdot960}}{2}
   =\frac{4\sqrt{30}\pm12\sqrt{30}}{2}
   =8\sqrt{30}\quad(\text{positive sum}).
\]

Now from (1),

\[
P=156+\frac{39}{\sqrt{30}}\,(8\sqrt{30})
   =156+312=468.
\]

Thus  

\[
bc = AB\cdot AC = 468.
\]

---

\[
\boxed{468}
\]

assistantfinalWe use the standard triangle formulas together with the given condition \(IA\perp OI\).

---

### 1.  Length \(OI\)

For any triangle  

\[
OI^{2}=R(R-2r).
\]

With \(R=13,\;r=6\),

\[
OI^{2}=13\bigl(13-12\bigr)=13\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad OI=\sqrt{13}.
\]

---

### 2.  Length \(IA\)

Since \(IA\perp OI\), triangle \(AIO\) is right‑angled at \(I\).  
Hence

\[
OA^{2}=OI^{2}+IA^{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
13^{2}=13+IA^{2},
\]

so  

\[
IA^{2}=169-13=156\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad IA=2\sqrt{39}.
\]

---

### 3.  Angle \(A\)

The distance from the incenter to a vertex satisfies  

\[
IA=\frac{r}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}.
\]

Thus  

\[
\frac{6}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}=2\sqrt{39}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\sin\frac{A}{2}= \frac{6}{2\sqrt{39}}=\frac{\sqrt{39}}{13}.
\]

Consequently  

\[
\cos\frac{A}{2}= \sqrt{1-\sin^{2}\frac{A}{2}}
               =\sqrt{1-\frac{39}{169}}
               =\frac{\sqrt{130}}{13},
\]
\[
\sin A = 2\sin\frac{A}{2}\cos\frac{A}{2}
       =\frac{2\sqrt{39}}{13}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{130}}{13}
       =\frac{2\sqrt{30}}{13},
\qquad
\cos A =1-2\sin^{2}\frac{A}{2}= \frac{91}{169}.
\]

---

### 4.  Side \(a=BC\)

From the law of sines  

\[
a=2R\sin A =2\cdot13\cdot\frac{2\sqrt{30}}{13}=4\sqrt{30}.
\]

---

### 5.  Semiperimeter \(s\)

A useful identity for the inradius is  

\[
r=(s-a)\tan\frac{A}{2}.
\]

Since  

\[
\tan\frac{A}{2}= \frac{\sin\frac{A}{2}}{\cos\frac{A}{2}}
               =\frac{\sqrt{39}}{\sqrt{130}}
               =\sqrt{\frac{3}{10}}=\frac{\sqrt{30}}{10},
\]

we obtain  

\[
6=(s-a)\frac{\sqrt{30}}{10}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
s-a= \frac{60}{\sqrt{30}}=2\sqrt{30}.
\]

With \(a=4\sqrt{30}\),

\[
s = a+2\sqrt{30}=4\sqrt{30}+2\sqrt{30}=6\sqrt{30}.
\]

---

### 6.  Product \(AB\cdot AC\)

Let \(b=AC\) and \(c=AB\).  
Using \(R=\dfrac{abc}{4\Delta}\) and \(\Delta=rs\),

\[
13 =\frac{abc}{4\,(6s)}\;\Longrightarrow\; abc = 13\cdot24s =312s.
\]

Hence  

\[
bc=\frac{312s}{a}= \frac{312\,(6\sqrt{30})}{4\sqrt{30}}
   =\frac{1872\sqrt{30}}{4\sqrt{30}} = 468.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\boxed{AB\cdot AC = 468 }.
\]

### 1.  Using the perpendicular condition

\[

But for any triangle

\]

Thus  

\[
AI^{2}=R^{2}-OI^{2}=R^{2}-R(R-2r)=2Rr.
\]

With \(R=13,\;r=6\),

\[
AI^{2}=2\cdot13\cdot6=156\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad AI=2\sqrt{39}.
\]

Since the distance from the incenter to a vertex is  

\[
AI=\frac{r}{\sin\frac{A}{2}},
\]

we obtain  

\[
\sin\frac{A}{2}=\frac{r}{AI}=\frac{6}{2\sqrt{39}}=\frac{\sqrt{39}}{13},
\qquad
\cos\frac{A}{2}=\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}\frac{A}{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{130}}{13}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\sin A=2\sin\frac{A}{2}\cos\frac{A}{2}

\]

The length of the tangent from \(A\) to the incircle equals

\sqrt{AI^{2}-r^{2}}=\sqrt{156-36}= \sqrt{120}=2\sqrt{30}.
\]

But this tangent length is precisely \(s-a\) (the distance from \(A\) to the point of tangency on \(AB\) or \(AC\)).  
Therefore  

\[
s-a=2\sqrt{30}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad s=a+2\sqrt{30}=4\sqrt{30}+2\sqrt{30}=6\sqrt{30}.
\]

---

### 4.  Area of the triangle  

\[
\Delta = rs = 6\cdot6\sqrt{30}=36\sqrt{30}.
\]

### 5.  Find \(b\cdot c = AB\cdot AC\)

Using \(\displaystyle \Delta=\frac12 bc\sin A\),

\[
\frac12\,bc\sin A = 36\sqrt{30}

bc = \frac{72\sqrt{30}}{\sin A}.

\[

    = 72\sqrt{30}\cdot\frac{13}{2\sqrt{30}}

\[
\boxed{AB\cdot AC = 468}.

IA^{2}=OA^{2}-OI^{2}=R^{2}-R(R-2r)=2Rr .

The distance from the incenter to a vertex is

Therefore

a = 2R\sin A =2\cdot13\cdot\frac{2\sqrt{30}}{13}=4\sqrt{30}.

\[

so

The area \(\Delta\) satisfies \(\Delta = rs\) and also \(\Delta=\dfrac{abc}{4R}\).

\[

Hence

\[
bc=\frac{4Rrs}{a}

\]

\[
\cos\frac A2=\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}\frac A2}

\sin A=2\sin\frac A2\cos\frac A2
      =\frac{2\sqrt{30}}{13},

\[

\tag{1}
\]

\]

\[
\frac{B}{2}=\frac{\pi-A}{2}+\delta,\qquad

   =\frac{130}{169}\cos^{2}\!\delta-\frac{39}{169}\sin^{2}\!\delta.

\frac{130}{169}\cos^{2}\!\delta-\frac{39}{169}\sin^{2}\!\delta

### 3.  Relate \(b+c\) and \(bc\) to \(\cos\delta\)

    =4R\sin\frac{B+C}{2}\cos\delta

### 4.  Determine \(\cos\delta\)

From (2) we obtain a quadratic for \(\cos\delta\):
\[

\]
whose solutions are

Insert \(\cos\delta=\dfrac{2\sqrt{39}}{13}\) into (4):

\[

   =156+52\cdot\frac{2\cdot39}{13}
   =156+52\cdot6
   =156+312

\]

\[
AB\cdot AC=bc= \boxed{468}.
\]

Let  

\[
S_1=a+b+c,\qquad S_2=ab+bc+ca,\qquad S_3=abc .
\]

For any three numbers the identity  

\[
a^2b+b^2c+c^2a+a b^2+b c^2+c a^2
      =S_1S_2-3S_3
\]

holds (expand \((a+b+c)(ab+bc+ca)\)).  
In our problem  

\[
S_1=300,\qquad S_1S_2-3S_3=6\,000\,000 .
\]

Hence  

\[
300S_2-3S_3=6\,000\,000\;\Longrightarrow\;
100S_2-S_3=2\,000\,000\qquad (1)
\]

and  

\[
S_3=abc=100S_2-2\,000\,000. \tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Solutions with a zero component  

If one of \(a,b,c\) is \(0\), then \(S_3=0\) and (2) gives \(S_2=20\,000\).  
With, say, \(c=0\) we have \(a+b=300\) and \(ab=S_2=20\,000\).  
Thus  

\[
a(300-a)=20\,000\;\Longrightarrow\;a^2-300a+20\,000=0
\]

whose integer solutions are \(a=200,\;100\).  
Hence the triples with a zero entry are  

\[
(200,100,0),\;(100,200,0)
\]

and all their permutations – **\(6\) ordered triples**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Solutions with all components positive  

Now \(a,b,c>0\).  From (2) we have  

\[
abc=100(ab+bc+ca)-2\,000\,000. \tag{3}
\]

Because the cubic  

\[
x^3-300x^2+S_2x-(100S_2-2\,000\,000)=0
\]

has integer roots \(a,b,c\), each of them must divide the constant term
\(2\,000\,000=2^{7}\cdot5^{6}\).  Hence every positive component belongs to  

\[
\{1,2,4,5,8,10,16,20,25,32,40,50,64,80,100,125,128,160,200,250\}.
\]

Searching all triples from this set whose sum is \(300\) and that satisfy
(3) yields only two possibilities:

* \(a=b=c=100\);
* \(\{a,b,c\}=\{100,40,160\}\).

Both indeed satisfy (3) (for \((100,100,100)\): \(S_2=30\,000,\;S_3=1\,000\,000\);
for \((100,40,160)\): \(S_2=26\,400,\;S_3=640\,000\)).  

The triple \((100,100,100)\) is a single ordered triple, while the three
distinct numbers \(100,40,160\) give \(3! = 6\) ordered triples.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Total number of triples

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{type of solution} & \text{ordered triples} \\ \hline
\text{one zero entry} & 6\\
(100,100,100) & 1\\
(100,40,160)\ \text{(all distinct)} & 6\\ \hline
\text{Total} & 13
\end{array}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{13}
\]

### 1.  Reformulating the second condition  

\[
\begin{aligned}

\]

Hence  

\[

\tag{1}
\]

where  

\[
S_2=a^2+b^2+c^2,\qquad S_3=a^3+b^3+c^3 .
\]

---

### 2.  Using the identity for the cube of a sum  

\[
(a+b+c)^3=a^3+b^3+c^3+3(a+b)(b+c)(c+a).
\]

\[

\]

\tag{3}
\]

---

### 3.  A convenient change of variables  

Set  

\[
A=300-a,\qquad B=300-b,\qquad C=300-c .
\]

\[

\]

\[
100\bigl[-90\,000+(A^2+B^2+C^2)\bigr]=11\,000\,000-ABC,
\]

or after simplifying

\[
100\,(A^2+B^2+C^2)+ABC=20\,000\,000.
\tag{4}
\]

\[

\]

\[
\boxed{7}.

Let  

\[
a,b,c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0},\qquad a+b+c=300,
\]

and  

\[
a^{2}b+a^{2}c+b^{2}a+b^{2}c+c^{2}a+c^{2}b=6\,000\,000 .
\tag{1}
\]

---

### 1.  Express the symmetric sum in terms of the elementary symmetric sums  

Recall the identity  

\[
(a+b+c)^{3}=a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}+3\bigl(a^{2}b+a^{2}c+b^{2}a+b^{2}c+c^{2}a+c^{2}b\bigr)+6abc .
\]

With \(a+b+c=300\) we have \((a+b+c)^{3}=300^{3}=27\,000\,000\).  
Hence from (1)

\[
\begin{aligned}
27\,000\,000
&=a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}+3\cdot6\,000\,000+6abc\\
&=a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}+18\,000\,000+6abc .
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore  

\[
a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}+6abc=9\,000\,000 .
\tag{2}
\]

Write the elementary symmetric sums  

\[
S_{1}=a+b+c=300,\qquad 
S_{2}=ab+bc+ca,\qquad 
S_{3}=abc .
\]

The well‑known identity  

\[
a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}=S_{1}^{3}-3S_{1}S_{2}+3S_{3}
\]

gives, after substituting \(S_{1}=300\) into (2),

\[
27\,000\,000-3\cdot300\;S_{2}+3S_{3}+6S_{3}=9\,000\,000 .
\]

Simplifying,

\[
-900\,S_{2}+9S_{3}=-18\,000\,000\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
S_{3}=100\,S_{2}-2\,000\,000 .
\tag{3}
\]

But \(S_{3}=abc\) and \(S_{2}=ab+bc+ca\).  Substituting these into (3) yields

\[
abc=100\,(ab+bc+ca)-2\,000\,000 .
\tag{4}
\]

---

### 2.  Factorisation

Observe that  

\[
(a-100)(b-100)(c-100)
=abc-100(ab+bc+ca)+100^{2}(a+b+c)-100^{3}.
\]

Since \(a+b+c=300\) and \(100^{2}\cdot300-100^{3}=3\,000\,000-1\,000\,000=2\,000\,000\),

\[
(a-100)(b-100)(c-100)=abc-100(ab+bc+ca)+2\,000\,000 .
\]

Using (4) we have \(abc-100(ab+bc+ca)=-2\,000\,000\), therefore

\[
(a-100)(b-100)(c-100)=0 .
\tag{5}
\]

Thus **at least one of the numbers \(a,b,c\) equals \(100\).**  
Conversely, any non‑negative triple with sum \(300\) and with one entry equal to \(100\) satisfies (5) and therefore (1).  

Hence the original problem is equivalent to:

> Find the non‑negative integer solutions of \(a+b+c=300\) with at least one coordinate equal to \(100\).

---

### 3.  Counting the solutions

*Fix a coordinate to be \(100\).*  

- If \(a=100\), then \(b+c=200\). The number of non‑negative solutions \((b,c)\) is \(200+1=201\).  
- The same count holds for \(b=100\) and for \(c=100\).

Thus the naive count is \(3\times201=603\).

The triple \((100,100,100)\) has been counted three times (once for each choice of the coordinate set to \(100\)).  We must subtract the two extra copies:

\[
603-2 = 601 .
\]

---

### 4.  Answer

\[
\boxed{601}
\]

\end{aligned}
\]

The required equality becomes  

\[
300\,s_2-s_3=6\,000\,000 .

Using the identities for \(s_2\) and \(s_3\) in terms of \(a,b,c\),

\[
s_2=ab+bc+ca,\qquad s_3=abc,

\[
300(ab+bc+ca)-abc=6\,000\,000 .

\[

\[

\]

and \(p\) and \(q\) are relatively prime.

\[
\boxed{p+q=7+16=23}.

assistantfinalThe family \(\mathcal{F}\) consists of the line segments joining \((a,0)\) to \((0,b)\) with  

\[
a^{2}+b^{2}=1,\qquad a>0,\;b>0 .
\]

Any point \((x,y)\) on such a segment satisfies the intercept form  

\[
\frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=1\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad bx+ay=ab .
\]

Writing \(a=\cos\theta,\;b=\sin\theta\;(0<\theta<\pi/2)\) gives the one‑parameter family of lines  

\[
\sin\theta\,x+\cos\theta\,y=\sin\theta\cos\theta .
\tag{1}
\]

The segment \(\overline{AB}\) itself corresponds to \(\theta_{0}= \pi/3\) because  

\[
A=\Bigl(\tfrac12,0\Bigr)=\bigl(\cos\frac{\pi}{3},0\bigr),\qquad 
B=\Bigl(0,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\Bigr)=\bigl(0,\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\bigr).
\]

Hence the line through \(A\) and \(B\) is  

\[
\frac{x}{\frac12}+\frac{y}{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}=1
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
\frac{\sqrt3}{2}x+\frac12y=\frac{\sqrt3}{4},
\]

which is exactly (1) with \(\theta=\pi/3\).

---

### When does a point on \(\overline{AB}\) lie on another segment of \(\mathcal{F}\)?

For a fixed point \((x,y)\) we ask for the number of \(\theta\in(0,\pi/2)\) satisfying (1).  
Define  

\[
F(\theta)=\sin\theta\,x+\cos\theta\,y-\sin\theta\cos\theta .
\]

A point belongs to at least one segment of \(\mathcal{F}\) iff \(F(\theta)=0\) for some \(\theta\).  
On \(\overline{AB}\) we already have a solution \(\theta_{0}=\pi/3\) (the line \(\overline{AB}\) itself).  
If a second distinct segment passes through the same point, then (1) has a second root \(\theta\neq\pi/3\).

The unique interior point \(C\) that lies on **no** other segment is precisely the point where
\(\theta=\pi/3\) is a *double* root of \(F\); i.e. both  

\[
F(\pi/3)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad F'(\pi/3)=0
\]

must hold.

Compute the derivative:

\[
F'(\theta)=\cos\theta\,x-\sin\theta\,y-\cos2\theta .
\]

Evaluating at \(\theta=\pi/3\) (\(\sin\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\;\cos\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac12,\;
\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}=-\frac12\)) gives  

\[
F'(\tfrac{\pi}{3})=\tfrac12\,x-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\,y+\tfrac12=0
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
x-\sqrt3\,y+1=0. \tag{2}
\]

Points on \(\overline{AB}\) satisfy its line equation  

\[
\frac{x}{\frac12}+\frac{y}{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}=1
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
2x+\frac{2}{\sqrt3}y=1. \tag{3}
\]

\[
\begin{cases}
x-\sqrt3\,y+1=0,\\[2mm]
2x+\frac{2}{\sqrt3}y=1,
\end{cases}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
y=\frac{3\sqrt3}{8},\;\;x=\frac18 .
\]

Thus  

\[
C=\Bigl(\frac18,\;\frac{3\sqrt3}{8}\Bigr)
\]

is the unique interior point of \(\overline{AB}\) that lies on no segment of \(\mathcal{F}\) other than \(\overline{AB}\).

\[

      =\frac{1}{64}+\frac{27}{64}
      =\frac{28}{64}
      =\frac{7}{16}.
\]

\[
\boxed{p+q = 7+16 = 23}
\]

\[
p^{2}+q^{2}=1 ,\qquad p,q>0 .
\]

Writing \(p=\cos\theta ,\;q=\sin\theta\;(0<\theta<\tfrac{\pi}{2})\), the line containing such a segment is  

\[
L_{\theta}:\; y=-\tan\theta\,x+\sin\theta .
\]

All these lines form a one‑parameter family.  
The envelope of a family of lines \(F(x,y,\theta)=0\) is obtained from  

\[
F(x,y,\theta)=0,\qquad \frac{\partial F}{\partial\theta}=0 .
\]

Here  

\[
F(x,y,\theta)=y+\tan\theta\,x-\sin\theta .
\]

Differentiating with respect to \(\theta\),

\[
\frac{\partial F}{\partial\theta}=x\sec^{2}\theta-\cos\theta=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x=\cos^{3}\theta .
\]

Substituting this into the line equation gives  

\[
y=-\tan\theta\cos^{3}\theta+\sin\theta
   =\sin^{3}\theta .
\]

Hence the envelope is the curve  

\[
x=\cos^{3}\theta ,\qquad y=\sin^{3}\theta\qquad(0<\theta<\tfrac{\pi}{2}),
\]
or, eliminating \(\theta\),

\[
x^{\frac{2}{3}}+y^{\frac{2}{3}}=1 .
\]

Each line \(L_{\theta}\) touches the envelope at the unique point
\((\cos^{3}\theta,\sin^{3}\theta)\).  
That point lies on the corresponding segment and on no other segment of the family.

For the given segment \(AB\) we have  

\[
A=\Bigl(\frac12,0\Bigr),\qquad B=\Bigl(0,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\Bigr),
\]
so \(\cos\theta_{0}= \frac12,\; \sin\theta_{0}= \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\) (i.e. \(\theta_{0}=60^{\circ}\)).  
The tangency point on \(AB\) is therefore  

\[
C=\bigl(\cos^{3}\theta_{0},\;\sin^{3}\theta_{0}\bigr)
   =\Bigl(\frac{1}{2^{3}},\;\frac{(\sqrt3)^{3}}{2^{3}}\Bigr)
   =\Bigl(\frac18,\;\frac{3\sqrt3}{8}\Bigr).
\]

Indeed \(C\) lies on \(AB\) because  

\[
\sqrt3\cdot\frac18+\frac{3\sqrt3}{8}
   =\frac{\sqrt3}{2},
\]
the equation of the line through \(A\) and \(B\).

Now compute the squared distance from the origin:

\[
OC^{2}= \Bigl(\frac18\Bigr)^{2}+\Bigl(\frac{3\sqrt3}{8}\Bigr)^{2}
      =\frac{1}{64}+\frac{27}{64}
      =\frac{28}{64}

Thus  

\[
OC^{2}= \frac{p}{q}\quad\text{with}\quad p=7,\;q=16,
\]
and \(p\) and \(q\) are relatively prime.

\[
\boxed{p+q=7+16=23}
\]

|AB|=\sqrt{\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)^2+\Bigl(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\Bigr)^2}=1 .
\]

Hence \(AB\) itself belongs to the family \(\mathcal F\) (the unique segment whose
end‑points are on the axes and have length 1).

---

### 1.  Equation of a generic segment in \(\mathcal F\)

If a segment \(\overline{PQ}\in\mathcal F\) has \(P=(p,0)\) and \(Q=(0,q)\) with
\(p,q>0\), the length condition gives  

\[
p^{2}+q^{2}=1 .
\]

The line through \(P\) and \(Q\) has intercept form  

\[
\frac{x}{p}+\frac{y}{q}=1\qquad (p^{2}+q^{2}=1). \tag{1}
\]

---

### 2.  Points of \(\overline{AB}\)

A point on \(\overline{AB}\) can be written as  

\[
(x,y)=\Bigl(\frac{1-t}{2},\; \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\,t\Bigr),\qquad 0\le t\le1 .
\tag{2}
\]

(Here \(t=0\) gives \(A\), \(t=1\) gives \(B\).)

---

### 3.  When does a point of \(\overline{AB}\) lie on another line of \(\mathcal F\)?

Substituting \((x,y)\) from (2) into (1) gives, for a given \(t\),

\[
\frac{\displaystyle\frac{1-t}{2}}{p}
\;+\;
\frac{\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\,t}{q}=1,
\qquad p^{2}+q^{2}=1 .
\tag{3}
\]

Write \(p=\cos\theta,\;q=\sin\theta\;(0<\theta<\tfrac\pi2)\).  
Then (3) becomes  

\[
\frac{1-t}{2}\,\sec\theta
\;+\;
\frac{t\sqrt3}{2}\,\csc\theta=1 .
\tag{4}
\]

Multiplying by \(2\),

\[
(1-t)\sec\theta +t\sqrt3\,\csc\theta =2 . \tag{5}
\]

For each fixed \(t\) we ask whether (5) has a solution \(\theta\neq\frac\pi3\)
(the case \(\theta=\frac\pi3\) corresponds to the original segment \(AB\)).
Define  

\[
F(\theta)= (1-t)\sec\theta +t\sqrt3\,\csc\theta .
\]

On \((0,\frac\pi2)\) we have \(F(\theta)\to\infty\) as \(\theta\to0^+\) and as
\(\theta\to\frac\pi2^{-}\).  Moreover \(F\!\bigl(\frac\pi3\bigr)=2\) for every
\(t\).  Thus the level \(F(\theta)=2\) will intersect the curve a second time
iff the minimum of \(F\) is **strictly below** 2.  The unique interior point of

the minimum of \(F\) is exactly 2; then the line \(AB\) is tangent to the
envelope of the family.

Set the derivative of \(F\) to zero at \(\theta=\frac\pi3\):

\[
F'(\theta)=-(1-t)\sec\theta\tan\theta
          -t\sqrt3\,\csc\theta\cot\theta .
\]

Evaluating at \(\theta=\frac\pi3\) (\(\sec\frac\pi3=2,\;\tan\frac\pi3=\sqrt3,
\;\csc\frac\pi3= \tfrac{2}{\sqrt3},\;\cot\frac\pi3=\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\)) gives  

\[
F'\!\Bigl(\frac\pi3\Bigr)=
-(1-t)\,2\sqrt3
-\;t\sqrt3\;\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\;\frac1{\sqrt3}
= -2\sqrt3\,(1-t) -\frac{2t}{\sqrt3}.
\]

Setting this equal to \(0\) yields  

\[
-2\sqrt3\,(1-t)-\frac{2t}{\sqrt3}=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
t=\frac34 .
\]

Thus the only point of \(\overline{AB}\) for which the line \(AB\) is tangent to
the envelope (and hence belongs to no other segment of \(\mathcal F\)) is the
point corresponding to \(t=\tfrac34\).

---

### 4.  Coordinates of the special point \(C\)

From (2) with \(t=\frac34\),

\[
C=\Bigl(\frac{1-\frac34}{2},\;\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\frac34\Bigr)
   =\Bigl(\frac18,\;\frac{3\sqrt3}{8}\Bigr).
\]

Indeed \(C\) lies on \(\overline{AB}\) and is distinct from \(A\) and \(B\).

---

### 5.  Compute \(OC^{2}\)

\[
OC^{2}= \left(\frac18\right)^{2}
        +\left(\frac{3\sqrt3}{8}\right)^{2}
      =\frac1{64}+\frac{27}{64}
      =\frac{28}{64}
      =\frac7{16}.
\]

Thus \(OC^{2}=\dfrac{p}{q}\) with relatively prime positive integers
\(p=7,\;q=16\).

\[
p+q = 7+16 = \boxed{23}.
\]

assistantfinalThe family \(\mathcal F\) consists of all unit‑segments whose endpoints lie on the coordinate axes.  
If the endpoint on the \(x\)-axis is \((p,0)\) and the endpoint on the \(y\)-axis is \((0,q)\) then

\[
p>0,\;q>0,\qquad p^{2}+q^{2}=1 .
\]

The line containing such a segment satisfies  

\[
\frac{x}{p}+\frac{y}{q}=1\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta=\sin\theta\cos\theta,
\]

where we set \(p=\cos\theta,\;q=\sin\theta\) (\(\theta\in(0,\pi/2)\)).  

Thus the family of lines is  

\[
F_\theta:\;x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta=\sin\theta\cos\theta .
\]

---

### Envelope of the family

A point that lies on **exactly one** line of the family must belong to the envelope of \(\{F_\theta\}\).  
The envelope is obtained from

\[
\begin{cases}
x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta=\sin\theta\cos\theta,\\[2pt]
\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\bigl(x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta-\sin\theta\cos\theta\bigr)=0,
\end{cases}
\]

i.e.

\[
\begin{cases}
x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta=\sin\theta\cos\theta,\\[2pt]
x\cos\theta-y\sin\theta=\cos^{2}\theta-\sin^{2}\theta .
\end{cases}
\]

Solving for \(x\) and \(y\) gives

\[
\boxed{x=\cos^{3}\theta,\qquad y=\sin^{3}\theta},
\]

the parametric equation of the astroid \(x^{2/3}+y^{2/3}=1\).

---

### Intersection with \(\overline{AB}\)

The segment \(\overline{AB}\) joins  

\[
A=\Bigl(\frac12,0\Bigr),\qquad B=\Bigl(0,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\Bigr),
\]

so its line equation is  

\[
y=-\sqrt3\,x+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.
\]

The unique point of \(\overline{AB}\) that lies on the envelope (hence on no other segment of \(\mathcal F\)) occurs for the \(\theta\) that produces the line \(AB\).  
Since \(A=(\cos\theta,0)\) and \(B=(0,\sin\theta)\) for this line, we have  

\[
\cos\theta=\frac12,\qquad \sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\;\Longrightarrow\;\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}.
\]

Plugging \(\theta=\pi/3\) into the envelope parametrisation:

\[
C=\bigl(\cos^{3}\tfrac{\pi}{3},\;\sin^{3}\tfrac{\pi}{3}\bigr)
   =\Bigl(\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)^{3},\;\Bigl(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\Bigr)^{3}\Bigr)
   =\left(\frac18,\;\frac{3\sqrt3}{8}\right).
\]

Indeed \(C\) lies on \(AB\) because  

\[
-\sqrt3\!\left(\frac18\right)+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}
   =\frac{3\sqrt3}{8}=y_{C}.
\]

---

### Distance \(OC\)

\[
OC^{2}= \left(\frac18\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{3\sqrt3}{8}\right)^{2}
       =\frac1{64}+\frac{27}{64}
       =\frac{28}{64}
       =\frac{7}{16}.
\]

Thus \(OC^{2}= \dfrac{7}{16}\), so \(p=7,\;q=16\) and

\[
\boxed{p+q=23}.
\]

### 1.  Points of \(\mathcal F\)

A segment \(\overline{PQ}\in\mathcal F\) has  

\[

### 2.  Points on \(\overline{AB}\)

A point \((u,v)\) lies on \(\overline{AB}\) iff  

\[
\frac{u}{\frac12}+\frac{v}{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}=1

2u+\frac{2}{\sqrt3}v=1,
\]

\[
v=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\bigl(1-2u\bigr),\qquad 0<u<\frac12. \tag{2}
\]

---

### 3.  When does a point of \(\overline{AB}\) belong to another segment of \(\mathcal F\)?

We ask whether there exist numbers \(x>0,\;y>0\) with  

\[
x^{2}+y^{2}=1\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{u}{x}+\frac{v}{y}=1. \tag{3}
\]

Set \(p=\dfrac1x,\;q=\dfrac1y\;(p,q>0)\).  
Then (3) becomes  

\[
up+vq=1,\qquad \frac1{p^{2}}+\frac1{q^{2}}=1. \tag{4}
\]

From the first equation \(q=\dfrac{1-up}{v}\). Substituting into the second gives a single

\[
\frac1{p^{2}}+\frac{v^{2}}{(1-up)^{2}}=1

\bigl(1-up\bigr)^{2}\bigl(p^{2}-1\bigr)=v^{2}p^{2}. \tag{5}
\]

\[
4a^{2}p^{4}-8ap^{3}+\bigl(1+12a-16a^{2}\bigr)p^{2}+8ap-4=0. \tag{6}
\]

\[
(p-2)\Bigl[\,4a^{2}p^{3}+8a(a-1)p^{2}+(1-4a)p+2\,\Bigr]=0. \tag{7}

Hence  

\[

\[

      =\Bigl(\frac18\Bigr)^{2}

      =\frac1{64}+\frac{27}{64}

Thus \(\displaystyle OC^{2}=\frac{7}{16}\), so \(p=7,\;q=16\) (already relatively
prime).

\[
p+q=7+16=23.
\]

\boxed{23}

\[

### 1.  Envelope of the family

\[
F(X,Y,\theta)=\sin\theta\,X+\cos\theta\,Y-\sin\theta\cos\theta .
\]

\[
F=0,\qquad \frac{\partial F}{\partial\theta}=0 .
\]

\[
\begin{cases}
\sin\theta\,X+\cos\theta\,Y=\sin\theta\cos\theta,\\[2mm]
\cos\theta\,X-\sin\theta\,Y=\cos2\theta .
\end{cases}
\]

Solving this linear system gives  

\[
X=\cos^{3}\theta,\qquad Y=\sin^{3}\theta .
\]

\[
X^{2/3}+Y^{2/3}=1,
\]

the quarter‑astroid in the first quadrant.

The segment \(\overline{AB}\) joins  

\[
A\Bigl(\frac12,0\Bigr),\qquad B\Bigl(0,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\Bigr),
\]

\[
y=\sqrt3\Bigl(\frac12-x\Bigr)\qquad(0\le x\le\tfrac12).
\]

A point \((x,y)\) on \(\overline{AB}\) that also lies on the envelope must satisfy  

\[
x^{2/3}+y^{2/3}=1,\qquad y=\sqrt3\Bigl(\frac12-x\Bigr).
\]

\[
x^{2/3}+3^{1/3}\Bigl(\frac12-x\Bigr)^{2/3}=1 .
\]

Set \(u=x^{1/3}\) and \(v=\bigl(\frac12-x\bigr)^{1/3}\); then  

\[
u^{2}+3^{1/3}v^{2}=1,\qquad u^{3}+v^{3}=\frac12 .
\]

Solving these equations gives the unique solution  

\[
u=\frac12,\qquad v=\frac{3^{1/3}}{2},
\]

so  

\[
x=u^{3}=\frac18,\qquad 
y=\sqrt3\Bigl(\frac12-\frac18\Bigr)=\frac{3\sqrt3}{8}.
\]

\[
C\Bigl(\frac18,\;\frac{3\sqrt3}{8}\Bigr).

\[

\]

\[
OC^{2}=\frac{p}{q}=\frac{7}{16},
\qquad p=7,\;q=16,

\]

and the condition “the two digits sum to \(\sqrt n\)” gives  

\[
a+c=k .
\]

Hence  

\[
k^{2}=a\,b+c=a\,b+(k-a)=a(b-1)+k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
a=\frac{k^{2}-k}{b-1}.
\]

Since \(a\) must be an integer,  

\[
b-1\mid k(k-1). \tag{1}
\]

Moreover \(a\ge1\) forces \(k\ge2\); the leading digit condition also forces  

\[
k\le b-1\qquad\text{(otherwise the second digit would be negative).}
\]

Thus for a fixed \(b\) we have to count the integers  

\[
k\in\{2,3,\dots ,b-1\}
\]

satisfying (1).  Write \(m=b-1\).  Condition (1) is  

\[
m\mid k(k-1).
\]

Because \(\gcd(k,k-1)=1\), each prime power \(p^{e}\) dividing \(m\) must divide
either \(k\) or \(k-1\) (but not both).  Consequently, for every distinct prime
factor of \(m\) there are exactly two possibilities for \(k\) modulo that
prime power:  

\[
k\equiv0\pmod{p^{e}}\quad\text{or}\quad k\equiv1\pmod{p^{e}} .
\]

By the Chinese Remainder Theorem the total number of residues modulo \(m\)
satisfying (1) is  

\[
2^{\omega(m)},
\]

where \(\omega(m)\) is the number of distinct prime factors of \(m\).
Among these residues the one congruent to \(1\) corresponds to \(k=1\), which
does not give a two‑digit number, so the admissible values of \(k\) are  

\[
2^{\omega(m)}-1 .
\]

Thus the number of \(b\)-eautiful integers equals  

\[
\boxed{2^{\omega(b-1)}-1 }.
\]

We need this quantity to exceed \(10\):

\[
2^{\omega(b-1)}-1>10\;\Longleftrightarrow\;2^{\omega(b-1)}\ge12.
\]

The smallest exponent giving at least \(12\) is \(\omega(b-1)=4\) (since
\(2^{3}=8<12\) and \(2^{4}=16\ge12\)).  Hence \(b-1\) must have at least four
distinct prime factors.

The smallest integer with four distinct prime factors is the product of the
four smallest primes:

\[
b-1=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7=210.
\]

Therefore the smallest \(b\) for which there are more than ten \(b\)-eautiful
integers is  

\[
\boxed{b=210+1=211}.
\]

Indeed, for \(b=211\) we have \(\omega(b-1)=4\) and the count of
\(b\)-eautiful integers is \(2^{4}-1=15>10\).

Let the base be \(b\ge 2\) and write a two‑digit number \(n\) in base \(b\) as  

\[
n = a\,b + c ,\qquad 
1\le a\le b-1,\;0\le c\le b-1 .
\]

The “\(b\)-eautiful’’ condition is  

\[
a+c=\sqrt n .
\]

Set  

\[
s:=\sqrt n \qquad(\text{so }s\in\mathbb N,\;n=s^{2}),
\]

and write \(c=s-a\).  Substituting \(n=a b+c\) gives  

\[
a b + (s-a)=s^{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
a(b-1)=s^{2}-s=s(s-1).
\]

Hence  

\[
a=\frac{s(s-1)}{b-1}.
\tag{1}
\]

Because \(a\) must be an integer, the denominator \(d:=b-1\) must divide \(s(s-1)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Divisibility condition

Since consecutive integers are coprime, every prime factor of \(d\) must divide
either \(s\) or \(s-1\) (but not both).  Thus for each prime power
\(p^{e}\|d\) we have  

\[
s\equiv 0\pmod{p^{e}}\quad\text{or}\quad s\equiv 1\pmod{p^{e}} .
\tag{2}
\]

Conversely, any integer \(s\) satisfying (2) makes \(d\mid s(s-1)\).
The Chinese Remainder Theorem shows that (2) determines a unique residue
class modulo \(d\) for each choice of “\(0\)” or “\(1\)” for the distinct
prime powers dividing \(d\).  If \(d\) has \(\omega(d)\) distinct prime
factors, there are exactly  

\[
2^{\omega(d)}
\]

solutions of (2) modulo \(d\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Admissible values of \(s\)

The digit \(a\) must satisfy \(1\le a\le d\).  From (1),

\[
a=\frac{s(s-1)}{d}\ge 1\iff s(s-1)\ge d,
\]

which is automatic for any solution of (2) with \(s\ge 2\) (the only
solutions with \(s(s-1)<d\) are \(s=0,1\)).  
Also \(a\le d\) gives \(s(s-1)\le d^{2}\), i.e. \(s\le d\).

Thus the admissible values of \(s\) are the integers  

\[
2\le s\le d\quad\text{that satisfy }d\mid s(s-1).
\]

Among the \(2^{\omega(d)}\) residue classes given by (2), the class
\(s\equiv 1\pmod d\) yields \(s=1\), which is not allowed (it would give
\(a=0\)).  All the remaining \(2^{\omega(d)}-1\) classes give a unique
\(s\) in the interval \(2\le s\le d\).  Hence the number of
\(b\)-eautiful integers equals  

\[
N(b)=2^{\omega(b-1)}-1 .
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  When does \(N(b)>10\)?

We need  

\[
2^{\omega(b-1)}-1>10\;\Longleftrightarrow\;2^{\omega(b-1)}\ge 12.
\]

Since \(2^{3}=8<12\) and \(2^{4}=16>12\), we must have  

\[
\omega(b-1)\ge 4 .
\]

Thus \(b-1\) must have at least four distinct prime factors.
The smallest integer with four distinct prime factors is the product of the
four smallest primes:

\[
b-1 = 2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7 = 210 .
\]

Consequently the smallest admissible base is  

\[
\boxed{b=210+1=211}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Verification

For \(b=211\) we have \(d=210\) with \(\omega(d)=4\).  By (3),

\[
N(211)=2^{4}-1=15>10,
\]

so there are indeed fifteen \(211\)-eautiful integers (corresponding to the
\(s\) values obtained from the \(2^{4}=16\) residue classes, the one with
\(s=1\) being excluded).

No smaller base can have \(\omega(b-1)\ge4\); any \(b<211\) gives
\(\omega(b-1)\le3\) and therefore at most \(2^{3}-1=7\) beautiful numbers,
which is not enough.

Hence the least integer \(b\ge2\) for which there are more than ten
\(b\)-eautiful integers is  

\[
\boxed{211}.
\]

Let a base \(b\ge 2\) be fixed and write a positive integer \(n\) in base \(b\) as  

\[
n=a\,b+c ,\qquad 1\le a\le b-1,\;0\le c\le b-1 .
\]

The definition of a \(b\text{-eautiful}\) number says that the two digits add up to
\(\sqrt n\).  Hence

\[
a+c=\sqrt n \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \sqrt n\in\mathbb Z .
\]

Put \(\sqrt n=s\;(s\in\mathbb N)\).  Then \(n=s^{2}\) and the two conditions become  

\[
\begin{cases}
a+b\,c=s,\\[2mm]
a\,b+c=s^{2}.
\end{cases}
\]

Eliminating \(c\) gives  

\[
a\,b+s-a=s^{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a(b-1)=s(s-1).
\tag{1}
\]

Thus  

\[
a=\frac{s(s-1)}{b-1},\qquad c=s-a.
\tag{2}
\]

Because \(a\) and \(c\) must be digits we need  

\[
1\le a\le b-1,\qquad 0\le c\le b-1 .
\tag{3}
\]

From (2) and (3) we obtain the following equivalent conditions on the
integer \(s\):

* \(b-1\mid s(s-1)\);  
* \(b-1\le s(s-1)\le (b-1)^{2}\);  
* \(s\le b\) (the inequality \(c\ge0\) gives \(s(b-s)\ge0\)).

Let  

\[
m:=b-1 .
\]

Then the conditions become  

\[
\boxed{m\mid s(s-1),\qquad m\le s(s-1)\le m^{2},\qquad 1<s\le m.}
\tag{4}
\]

---

### 1.  How many solutions can (4) have?

Write the prime factorisation  

\[
m=\prod_{i=1}^{k}p_i^{e_i}\qquad(k=\omega(m))
\]

(\(\omega(m)\) = number of distinct prime factors of \(m\)).
Since \(\gcd(s,s-1)=1\), each prime power \(p_i^{e_i}\) must divide
either \(s\) or \(s-1\), but not both.  Consequently

\[
s\equiv
\begin{cases}
0\pmod{p_i^{e_i}}\\[1mm]
\text{or}\\[1mm]
1\pmod{p_i^{e_i}}
\end{cases}
\qquad(i=1,\dots ,k).
\]

By the Chinese remainder theorem there are exactly \(2^{k}\) residues
\(s\pmod m\) satisfying \(m\mid s(s-1)\).  One of them is \(s\equiv1\pmod m\)
(which gives \(s=1\) and is not allowed because then \(a=0\));
the other \(2^{k}-1\) give admissible values of \(s\).

Thus the total number of \(b\)-eautiful integers equals the number of
solutions of (4), i.e.

\[
N(b)=2^{\,\omega(b-1)}-1\quad\text{(after discarding }s=1\text{)} .
\tag{5}
\]

The extra inequality \(s(s-1)\ge m\) eliminates only the very small
solutions.  For each factorisation \(m=u\cdot v\) with \(\gcd(u,v)=1\) we
obtain a pair of solutions:
\[
s_{1}\equiv0\pmod u,\;s_{1}\equiv1\pmod v,\qquad
s_{2}=m-s_{1}.
\]
Exactly one of the pair is \(\le m/2\); the other is \(\ge m/2\) and
therefore automatically satisfies \(s(s-1)\ge m\).  Consequently at
least half of the \(2^{\omega(m)}-1\) admissible solutions fulfil the
lower‑bound condition, and the total number of \(b\)-eautiful integers is
still given by (5).

Hence we need  

\[
2^{\,\omega(b-1)}-1>10\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
2^{\,\omega(b-1)}\ge 12 .
\]

The smallest exponent of two exceeding \(11\) is \(2^{4}=16\); therefore
\(\omega(b-1)\ge4\).  The smallest integer possessing four distinct prime
factors is  

\[
b-1=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7=210,
\]

so the smallest possible base is  

\[
\boxed{b=210+1=211}.
\]

---

### 2.  Verification for \(b=211\)

Here \(m=b-1=210\).  The \(2^{4}-1=15\) admissible values of \(s\) are
obtained from the \(2^{4}=16\) choices of assigning each prime factor of
\(210\) to the congruence \(s\equiv0\) or \(s\equiv1\).  They are

\[
\begin{aligned}
&s=15,21,36,70,85,91,105,106,120,126,141,175,190,196,210 .
\end{aligned}
\]

All satisfy \(s(s-1)\ge210\).  For each such \(s\) we have a distinct
\(b\)-eautiful integer \(n=s^{2}\) (e.g. \(s=15\) gives \(n=225\),
\(s=210\) gives \(n=44100\), etc.).  Thus there are \(15>10\) numbers
that are \(211\)-eautiful.

No smaller base can work, because any base \(b<211\) has \(b-1\) with at
most three distinct prime factors, giving at most \(2^{3}-1=7\) beautiful
numbers.

\[
\boxed{211}
\]

The “\(b\)-eautiful’’ condition is

\[
(a+c)^{2}=a b+c .

\]

Put \(s=a+c\).  Then \(c=s-a\) and (1) becomes

\]

\[
a\,d=s(s-1),\qquad 1\le a\le d,\;0\le s-a\le d .
\tag{3}
\]

Thus \(d\mid s(s-1)\).  Because \(\gcd(s,s-1)=1\), every divisor
\(d\) of the product must split as  

\[
d=d_{1}d_{2},\qquad d_{1}\mid s,\;d_{2}\mid(s-1),\;\gcd(d_{1},d_{2})=1.
\]

For each ordered coprime factorisation \(d=d_{1}d_{2}\) there is a unique

\[
s\equiv0\pmod{d_{1}},\qquad s\equiv1\pmod{d_{2}},

\[
\#\{(d_{1},d_{2})\mid d_{1}d_{2}=d,\;\gcd(d_{1},d_{2})=1,\;d_{1}>1\}

\]

where \(\omega(d)\) is the number of distinct prime factors of \(d=b-1\).

\]

Thus \(b-1\) must have at least four distinct prime factors.

\[

\]

\]

assistantfinalFor a base \(b\ge 2\) write a two–digit number as  

\[
n = a\,b + c ,\qquad 1\le a\le b-1,\;0\le c\le b-1 .
\]

The defining condition is  

\[
a+c=\sqrt n .
\]

Hence \(\sqrt n\) must be an integer; let \(\sqrt n=k\).  
Then

\[
\begin{cases}
a b + c = k^{2},\\[2mm]
a + c = k .
\end{cases}
\]

Eliminate \(c\) (\(c=k-a\)):

\[
a b + (k-a)=k^{2}
\Longrightarrow a(b-1)=k(k-1).
\]

Put \(d=b-1\).  Then

\[
a=\frac{k(k-1)}{d},\qquad 
1\le a\le d .
\tag{1}
\]

Thus \(d\mid k(k-1)\).  Because \(\gcd(k,k-1)=1\), for each prime power
\(p^{e}\|d\) we must have either \(p^{e}\mid k\) or \(p^{e}\mid(k-1)\).
Hence

\[
k\equiv 0\text{ or }1\pmod{p^{e}}\qquad\text{for every }p^{e}\|d .
\]

Consequently, for each distinct prime factor of \(d\) we have two
independent choices (0 or 1), giving

\[
\#\{k\pmod d : d\mid k(k-1)\}=2^{\,r},
\]

where \(r\) is the number of distinct prime factors of \(d\).

The solutions \(k\) lie in the interval \(1\le k\le d\) (since
\(a\le d\) forces \(k\le d\)).  The case \(k=1\) yields \(a=0\), which is
not allowed (the leading digit must be non‑zero).  All other residues
produce a valid pair \((a,c)\) with \(0\le c\le d\).

Hence the number of \(b\)-eautiful integers equals

\[
N(b)=2^{\,r}-1,
\]

where \(r\) is the number of distinct prime divisors of \(d=b-1\).

We need \(N(b)>10\), i.e.

\[
2^{\,r}-1>10\;\Longrightarrow\;2^{\,r}>11\;\Longrightarrow\;r\ge4 .
\]

Thus \(b-1\) must have at least four distinct prime factors.
The smallest integer with four distinct prime factors is  

\[
2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7=210 .
\]

Therefore the smallest base is  

\[
b = 210+1 = 211 .
\]

For \(b=211\) we indeed obtain \(2^{4}-1=15\) distinct \(b\)-eautiful
integers (the fifteen values of \(k\) satisfying the congruences, all
giving admissible digits).

\[
\boxed{211}
\]

For a base \(b\ge 2\) a positive integer \(n\) is called *\(b\)-eautiful* when  

\[
n = xb+y\qquad (1\le x\le b-1,\;0\le y\le b-1)
\]

has exactly two base‑\(b\) digits and  

\[
x+y=\sqrt n .
\]

Hence \(\sqrt n\) must be an integer; write \(\sqrt n = s\).  
Then

\[
n=s^{2}=xb+y,\qquad x+y=s. \tag{1}
\]

From (1) we obtain  

\[
s^{2}=xb+y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x+y)^{2}=xb+y .
\]

Since \(x+y=s\),

\[
s^{2}=xb+y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad s^{2}=xb+(s-x)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad xb=s^{2}-s+x .
\]

Thus  

\[
b=\frac{s^{2}-s+x}{x}=1+\frac{s(s-1)}{x}. \tag{2}
\]

Let  

\[
d=b-1.
\]

Equation (2) becomes  

\[
d=\frac{s(s-1)}{x}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=\frac{s(s-1)}{d}. \tag{3}
\]

Therefore a pair \((s,x)\) gives a \(b\)-eautiful number iff  

* \(d=b-1\) divides \(s(s-1)\);
* \(x=\dfrac{s(s-1)}{d}\) is an integer with \(1\le x\le d\);
* \(y=s-x\) satisfies \(0\le y\le d\).

The last two inequalities are automatically satisfied once \(1\le x\le d\)
(because then \(0\le y=s-x\le d\) follows from \(s\le d+1\); see below).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.   When does \(d\mid s(s-1)\)?

Write the prime factorisation  

\[
d=\prod_{i=1}^{\omega(d)}p_i^{e_i}\qquad(\omega(d)=\text{number of distinct primes}).
\]

Since \(\gcd(s,s-1)=1\), a prime power \(p_i^{e_i}\) must divide **either**
\(s\) or \(s-1\).  Consequently

\[
s\equiv 0\pmod{p_i^{e_i}}\quad\text{or}\quad s\equiv 1\pmod{p_i^{e_i}}
\qquad\text{for each }i .
\]

Hence the congruence  

\[
s(s-1)\equiv0\pmod d
\]

has exactly  

\[
2^{\omega(d)}
\]

solutions modulo \(d\) (one choice “0’’ or “1’’ for each distinct prime
factor).  Among these solutions two are \(s\equiv0\) and \(s\equiv1\); the
others lie strictly between \(0\) and \(d\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.   Which of those solutions give admissible \(s\)?

A \(b\)-eautiful integer must satisfy  

\[
b\le s^{2}\le b^{2}-1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\sqrt b\le s\le b-1 .
\]

Since \(b=d+1\), the admissible range for \(s\) is  

\[
\lceil\sqrt{d+1}\rceil\le s\le d .
\tag{4}
\]

All solutions of \(s(s-1)\equiv0\pmod d\) are distinct residues in
\(\{0,1,\dots ,d-1\}\).  For any \(d\ge2\) the two trivial solutions
\(s=0,1\) are smaller than the lower bound in (4).  Every other solution
lies in the interval \([2,d-1]\); as soon as the lower bound
\(\lceil\sqrt{d+1}\rceil\) exceeds \(2\) (which happens for every
\(b\ge5\)), **all** non‑trivial solutions are counted.

Thus the number of \(b\)-eautiful integers equals

\[
\#\{s:\; s(s-1)\equiv0\pmod d,\; s\ge\lceil\sqrt{d+1}\rceil\}
   = 2^{\omega(d)}-2 .
\tag{5}
\]

(The subtraction of \(2\) removes the inadmissible residues \(s=0,1\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.   Want more than ten \(b\)-eautiful numbers  

From (5) we need  

\[
2^{\omega(d)}-2>10\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
2^{\omega(d)}\ge 13 .
\]

The smallest power of two exceeding \(12\) is \(2^{4}=16\); therefore

\[
\omega(d)\ge4 .
\]

So \(d=b-1\) must have at least **four distinct prime factors**.
The smallest integer with four distinct prime factors is

\[
d=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7=210 .
\]

Consequently the smallest possible base is  

\[
b=d+1=210+1=211 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.   Verification for \(b=211\)

Here \(d=210\) and \(\omega(d)=4\); the admissible residues solving
\(s(s-1)\equiv0\pmod{210}\) are the \(2^{4}=16\) numbers

\[
s\equiv0\text{ or }1\pmod{2},\;
s\equiv0\text{ or }1\pmod{3},\;
s\equiv0\text{ or }1\pmod{5},\;
s\equiv0\text{ or }1\pmod{7}.
\]

All of them lie in \(\{0,1,\dots ,209\}\); only \(s=0\) and \(s=1\) are
below \(\lceil\sqrt{211}\rceil=15\).  Hence there are

\[
16-2=14>10
\]

different values of \(s\), giving the fourteen \(211\)-eautiful numbers

\[
s^{2}\;(s=15,\,21,\,25,\,35,\,42,\,49,\,63,\,70,\,84,\,105,\,126,
\,147,\,210,\,\dots )
\]

(all satisfying \(s^{2}= (s-1)\,211+1\) or the mixed‑congruence cases).

Thus \(b=211\) indeed yields more than ten \(b\)-eautiful integers, and any
smaller base cannot, because for \(b<211\) the integer \(b-1\) has at
most three distinct prime factors, giving at most \(2^{3}-2=6\) such
numbers.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{\,b_{\min}=211\,}
\]

Writing \(\sqrt n =k\) (so \(n=k^{2}\)) we obtain

k^{2}=x\,b+y,\qquad x+y=k .
\]

Eliminating \(y\) gives  

\[
k^{2}=x\,b+(k-x)=x(b-1)+k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad

\]

Hence  

\[
x=\frac{k(k-1)}{b-1},\qquad 
y=k-x .
\]

Thus a pair \((x,y)\) is admissible iff  

* \(b-1\mid k(k-1)\);
* \(1\le x\le b-1\) (which forces \(2\le k\le b-1\));
* \(0\le y\le b-1\) (automatically satisfied when the first two hold).

Since \(\gcd(k,k-1)=1\), each distinct prime factor of \(d\) can be assigned to either \(k\) or \(k-1\).

b=210+1=211.

\[
b-1\mid s(s-1).\tag{★}
\]

(When (★) holds, the formulas above give integer digits \(a,c\) and

### Counting the solutions

Put \(m=b-1\).  
Condition (★) is  

\[
m\mid s(s-1).
\]

Because \(\gcd(s,s-1)=1\), each prime power dividing \(m\) must divide
either \(s\) or \(s-1\).  
Consequently, for every distinct prime factor of \(m\) we have two
choices (assign the whole prime power to \(s\) or to \(s-1\)).
Hence the number of residues \(s\pmod m\) satisfying (★) is  

\[
2^{\omega(m)},
\]

where \(\omega(m)\) is the number of distinct prime factors of \(m\).

Thus for each odd prime factor we have two independent choices.

assistantfinalLet  

\[
n = d_1b+d_0\qquad (0\le d_0,d_1\le b-1,\;d_1>0)
\]

be a two‑digit number in base \(b\).  
The “\(b\)-eautiful’’ condition is  

\[
d_1+d_0=\sqrt n .
\]

Since \(\sqrt n\) is an integer, write \(\sqrt n=s\;(s\in\mathbb N)\).  
Then  

\[
n=s^{2}=d_1b+d_0,\qquad d_1+d_0=s .
\]

Eliminate \(d_0\;(=s-d_1)\):

\[
s^{2}=d_1b+(s-d_1)=d_1(b-1)+s
\Longrightarrow s^{2}-s=d_1(b-1).
\]

Hence  

\[
d_1=\frac{s(s-1)}{b-1}
\tag{1}
\]

must be an integer with \(1\le d_1\le b-1\).  
Because \(d_0=s-d_1\ge0\) and \(d_0\le b-1\) are automatically satisfied when
\(1\le d_1\le b-1\), the only condition is that  

\[
b-1\mid s(s-1). \tag{2}
\]

---

### How many \(s\) satisfy (2)?

Write \(m=b-1\).  
Since \(\gcd(s,s-1)=1\), (2) holds iff for every prime power \(p^{e}\| m\)
either \(p^{e}\mid s\) or \(p^{e}\mid s-1\).
Thus each distinct prime divisor of \(m\) gives two independent choices
(\(s\equiv0\) or \(1\pmod{p^{e}}\)).  

If \(m\) has \(\omega(m)\) distinct prime factors, the congruence
\(s(s-1)\equiv0\pmod m\) has exactly  

\[
2^{\omega(m)}
\]

solutions modulo \(m\).

The admissible values of \(s\) must also satisfy the two‑digit requirement

\[
b\le s^{2}\le b^{2}-1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 
\lceil\sqrt b\rceil\le s\le b-1=m .
\]

For a given \(m\) the interval \([\lceil\sqrt b\rceil,m]\) contains almost
all residues modulo \(m\); only the smallest few (less than \(\sqrt b\))
might be excluded.  Hence the number of \(b\)-eautiful integers is
essentially the number of solutions of (2) in that interval.

To have **more than ten** such integers we need  

\[
2^{\omega(m)}\ge 12\;\Longrightarrow\;\omega(m)\ge4 .
\]

The smallest integer with four distinct prime factors is  

\[
m=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7=210,
\]

so the smallest possible base is  

\[
b=m+1=211 .
\]

---

### Verification for \(b=211\)

Here \(m=210\) and \(\omega(m)=4\), so there are \(2^{4}=16\) residues
\(s\) modulo \(210\) satisfying \(210\mid s(s-1)\).  
The residues are  

\[
0,1,15,21,36,70,85,91,105,106,120,126,141,175,190,196\pmod{210}.
\]

Discarding \(s=0\) (which gives \(n=0\)) and keeping only those with
\(s\ge\lceil\sqrt{211}\rceil=15\) yields

\[
s=15,21,36,70,85,91,105,106,120,126,141,175,190,196,210,
\]

i.e. **15** admissible values.  Each gives a distinct
\(b\)-eautiful integer \(n=s^{2}\) (for example \(15^{2}=225,\;21^{2}=441,\dots\)).

Thus \(b=211\) indeed has more than ten \(b\)-eautiful integers.

No smaller base can have \(\omega(b-1)\ge4\); for any \(b<211\),
\(b-1\) has at most three distinct prime factors, giving at most
\(2^{3}=8\) solutions, far fewer than eleven.

\[
\boxed{\,b_{\min}=211\,}
\]

Let the vertices of the regular dodecagon be  

\[
V_{0},V_{1},\dots ,V_{11}
\qquad\text{with } 
V_{k}=e^{\,i\frac{2\pi k}{12}}\; .
\]

Every side or diagonal of the dodecagon is a chord joining two vertices
\(V_{p}\) and \(V_{q}\;(p\neq q)\).
A chord is completely determined by the *step*  

\[
k\equiv q-p\pmod{12},\qquad 1\le k\le 6 .
\]

(All chords with step \(k\) have the same length; the chord with step
\(12-k\) is the same line as the chord with step \(k\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Directions of the chords  

The direction (slope) of the chord joining \(V_{p}\) and \(V_{p+k}\) is

\[
\theta(p,k)=\frac{\arg V_{p}+\arg V_{p+k}}{2}+90^{\circ}
          =30p+15k+90^{\circ}\pmod{180^{\circ}} .
\]

For a fixed step \(k\) the six values of \(p=0,\dots ,5\) give six
different directions, spaced by \(30^{\circ}\).  
If we vary \(k\) we obtain only two families of directions:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{even }k\;(k=2,4,6)&:\;0^{\circ},30^{\circ},60^{\circ},
                         90^{\circ},120^{\circ},150^{\circ},\\[2mm]
\text{odd }k\;(k=1,3,5)&:\;15^{\circ},45^{\circ},75^{\circ},
                         105^{\circ},135^{\circ},165^{\circ}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus there are **twelve** distinct directions, occurring in two
interlaced 6‑tuples.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Parallel chords in a given direction  

For a fixed direction \(\alpha\) the equation  

\[
30p+15k+90\equiv\alpha\pmod{180}
\]

has exactly three solutions \((p,k)\) with \(0\le p\le5\) and
\(1\le k\le6\); consequently **three distinct chords** of the dodecagon
are parallel to any given direction \(\alpha\).

Hence each of the twelve directions supplies three parallel lines
inside the dodecagon.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Perpendicular direction pairs  

Two directions are perpendicular iff they differ by \(90^{\circ}\).
Because the directions are spaced by \(30^{\circ}\), the perpendicular
pairs are

\[
\begin{aligned}
&0^{\circ}\!\parallel\!90^{\circ},\;
30^{\circ}\!\parallel\!120^{\circ},\;
60^{\circ}\!\parallel\!150^{\circ},\\[1mm]
&15^{\circ}\!\parallel\!105^{\circ},\;
45^{\circ}\!\parallel\!135^{\circ},\;
75^{\circ}\!\parallel\!165^{\circ}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus there are **six** unordered perpendicular direction pairs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Forming a rectangle  

A rectangle is formed by choosing two parallel lines of one direction
and two parallel lines of the perpendicular direction; the four lines
intersect in four right‑angled corners.

For a given direction we have three parallel lines, so the number of
ways to pick two of them is  

\[
\binom{3}{2}=3 .
\]

The same count holds for the perpendicular direction.  Consequently,
for each perpendicular direction pair we obtain  

\[
\binom{3}{2}\times\binom{3}{2}=3\cdot3=9
\]

different rectangles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Total number of rectangles  

With six perpendicular direction pairs, the total number of rectangles
that can be drawn whose sides lie on sides or diagonals of the regular
dodecagon is

\[
6\;\times\;9 \;=\; \boxed{54}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Answer:** 54 rectangles can be formed inside a regular dodecagon with
each side of the rectangle lying on a side or a diagonal of the
dodecagon.

1. **Parallel families of chords**  
   In a regular 12‑gon every chord is determined by the sum of the indices of its two endpoints.  
   If the vertices are labelled \(0,1,\dots ,11\) (mod 12), the chord joining \(i\) and \(j\) belongs to the *parallel family* indexed by  

   \[
   s\equiv i+j\pmod{12}.
   \]

   Two chords are parallel iff they have the same value of \(s\).  
   There are 12 such families (slopes), each consisting of all chords with a given \(s\).

2. **How many chords in each family?**  
   For a fixed \(s\) there are \(\binom{12}{2}=66\) unordered pairs \(\{i,j\}\).  
   Solving \(i+j\equiv s\pmod{12}\) gives  

   * if \(s\) is **even**: 5 chords,  
   * if \(s\) is **odd** : 6 chords.

   (Indeed, for even \(s\) the unordered solutions are \((i,\,s-i)\) with \(i=1,2,3,4,5\); for odd \(s\) there are six such pairs.)

3. **Perpendicular families**  
   The direction of a chord in family \(s\) is  

   \[
   \theta_s=\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{\pi s}{12}.
   \]

   Two families are perpendicular when their directions differ by \(\pi/2\); this occurs exactly when their indices differ by 6:

   \[
   s\;\text{and}\;s+6\pmod{12}.
   \]

   Hence the 12 families split into the six perpendicular pairs  

   \[
   (0,6),\;(1,7),\;(2,8),\;(3,9),\;(4,10),\;(5,11).
   \]

4. **Forming a rectangle**  
   A rectangle is obtained by picking  

   * two *distinct* parallel chords from one family (the two opposite sides), and  
   * two *distinct* parallel chords from the perpendicular family (the other two opposite sides).

   \]

A rectangle inside a regular \(12\)-gon must have its four sides lie on chords of the polygon  
(sides are the chords of length 1, all other chords are diagonals).  
Hence the vertices of the rectangle are intersection points of those chords.  
Because the polygon is cyclic, a rectangle is a cyclic quadrilateral whose interior
angles are \(90^{\circ}\); consequently its two diagonals are diameters of the
circumscribed circle.  Equivalently, opposite sides of the rectangle are two **parallel**
chords of the same length, while the other pair of opposite sides are two parallel
chords of a different length, and the two families of chords are perpendicular.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Chords of a regular \(12\)-gon

Label the vertices \(V_{0},V_{1},\dots ,V_{11}\) counter‑clockwise.
A chord joining \(V_{i}\) to \(V_{i+k}\) (indices taken modulo 12) will be called a
**step‑\(k\) chord**.  

* For each step \(k\;(1\le k\le6)\) there are \(6\) distinct chords.
* The \(6\) chords of a given step fall into **three parallel pairs**:
  the chord \(V_{i}V_{i+k}\) is parallel to the chord \(V_{i+6}V_{i+6+k}\).
  Thus each step supplies exactly **three directions** of parallel chords.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  When are two families of chords perpendicular?

Let a step‑\(k\) chord have orientation  

\[
\theta_{k,i}= \frac{2\pi i}{12}+ \frac{k\pi}{12}+ \frac{\pi}{2}\qquad(i=0,1,2)
\]

(the three values of \(i\) give the three distinct directions for step \(k\)).
Two directions are perpendicular iff their orientations differ by \(\pi/2\)
(mod \(\pi\)).  Solving

\[
\theta_{k,i}-\theta_{\ell ,j}\equiv\frac{\pi}{2}\pmod{\pi}
\]

gives the condition  

\[
2(i-j)+(k-\ell)\equiv6\pmod{12}.
\]

Since \(i-j\) can be \(0,\pm1,\pm2\) (mod 3), this congruence has a solution
iff \(k-\ell\) is **even and non‑zero**.  Hence a step‑\(k\) family is perpendicular
to a step‑\(\ell\) family exactly when \(k\) and \(\ell\) have the same parity
(both odd or both even) and \(k\neq\ell\).

The admissible unordered pairs of steps are  

\[
\{1,3\},\{1,5\},\{3,5\}\qquad\text{(odd steps)}
\]
\[
\{2,4\},\{2,6\},\{4,6\}\qquad\text{(even steps)} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Counting the rectangles

For a fixed pair of steps \(\{k,\ell\}\) that are perpendicular:

* Step \(k\) offers **three** possible directions of parallel chords.
* Step \(\ell\) also offers **three** possible directions.
* For each choice of a direction of step \(k\) and a direction of step \(\ell\)
  that are perpendicular, the two parallel chords of step \(k\) together with the
  two parallel chords of step \(\ell\) intersect in exactly one rectangle.

The congruence above shows that, for any admissible pair \(\{k,\ell\}\), there are
exactly **three** perpendicular direction‑pairs.  Consequently each unordered
pair of steps yields \(3\) rectangles.

There are \(6\) admissible unordered step‑pairs, so the total number of rectangles is

\[
6\;\times\;3 \;=\; 18 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Answer

\[
\boxed{18}
\]

Thus a regular dodecagon contains exactly **18** distinct rectangles whose
sides lie on sides or diagonals of the polygon.

**Explanation (sketch of the counting argument)**  

1.  Number the vertices of the regular dodecagon \(0,1,\dots ,11\) in order around the circle.  
    Every side or diagonal is a chord joining two vertices \(\{i,j\}\) \((i<j)\).

2.  For a chord \(\{i,j\}\) the **orientation** of the line it lies on is determined by the
    sum \(s=i+j\pmod{12}\):
    \[
    \text{orientation }(\{i,j\})\equiv 15^{\circ}(i+j)-90^{\circ}
    \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
    s=i+j\pmod{12}.
    \]
    Hence all chords with the same value of \(s\) are parallel, and chords whose
    sums differ by \(6\) (i.e. \(s\) and \(s+6\)) are perpendicular.

3.  For each residue \(s\) there are  

    * \(5\) chords when \(s\) is even,  
    * \(6\) chords when \(s\) is odd.  

    (One checks this by listing the pairs \(\{i,j\}\) with \(i+j\equiv s\pmod{12}\).)

4.  A rectangle whose sides lie on chords must have its two opposite sides on two
    distinct parallel chords of one orientation and its other two opposite sides on
    two distinct parallel chords of the perpendicular orientation.  Thus a rectangle
    is determined uniquely by

    * a choice of two distinct chords from the “\(s\)‑family’’ (sum \(s\)), and  
    * a choice of two distinct chords from the “\(s+6\)‑family’’ (sum \(s+6\)).

    Because chords from the two families are perpendicular, any such four chords
    intersect pairwise in the required way and indeed form a rectangle (the four
    intersection points are the rectangle’s vertices).

5.  Consequently, for a fixed sum \(s\) the number of rectangles using the families
    \((s,\;s+6)\) is
    \[
    \binom{N_s}{2}\,\binom{N_{s+6}}{2},
    \]
    where \(N_s\) is the number of chords with sum \(s\).

    *If \(s\) is even*, \(N_s=N_{s+6}=5\), giving \(\binom{5}{2}^2=10^2=100\) rectangles.  
    *If \(s\) is odd*, \(N_s=N_{s+6}=6\), giving \(\binom{6}{2}^2=15^2=225\) rectangles.

6.  The sums \(s\) and \(s+6\) come in three even pairs \((0,6),(2,8),(4,10)\) and three
    odd pairs \((1,7),(3,9),(5,11)\).  Adding the contributions:

    \[
    \begin{aligned}
    \text{Even pairs: } &3\times 100 = 300,\\
    \text{Odd  pairs: } &3\times 225 = 675.
    \end{aligned}
    \]

    Hence the total number of rectangles is  

    \[
    300+675 = 975.
    \]

So there are **975** distinct rectangles whose sides lie on sides or diagonals of the regular dodecagon.

assistantfinal**Solution**

Let the vertices of the regular dodecagon be  
\[
V_{0},V_{1},\dots ,V_{11}
\]
in counter‑clockwise order (the angle between consecutive vertices is \(30^{\circ}\)).  
Any side or diagonal of the dodecagon is a line joining two vertices \(V_{i}\) and
\(V_{j}\;(i<j)\).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Directions of the chords  

For the chord \(V_iV_j\) the midpoint of the arc subtended at the centre is
\(\displaystyle\frac{i+j}{2}\cdot30^{\circ}\).  
The chord is perpendicular to the radius through that midpoint, hence its
direction angle (measured modulo \(180^{\circ}\)) is  

\[
\theta_{ij}= \frac{i+j}{2}\cdot30^{\circ}+90^{\circ}
          = (i+j)\cdot15^{\circ}+90^{\circ}\pmod{180^{\circ}} .
\]

Thus the direction of a chord depends only on the sum \(s=i+j\pmod{12}\).
Chords whose vertex–indices satisfy the same sum \(s\) are all parallel.

*If \(s\) is even* there is a degenerate “chord’’ \(V_{s/2}V_{s/2}\); the
remaining pairs give **5** genuine chords.  
*If \(s\) is odd* there is no such degenerate pair, giving **6** chords.

Hence for each residue \(s\;(0\le s\le11)\)

\[
N_s=\begin{cases}
5,&s\text{ even}\\[2mm]
6,&s\text{ odd}
\end{cases}
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Perpendicular families  

Two directions are perpendicular precisely when their direction angles differ
by \(90^{\circ}\).  
From the formula for \(\theta_{ij}\),

\[
\theta_{t}-\theta_{s}= (t-s)\cdot15^{\circ}\equiv90^{\circ}\pmod{180^{\circ}}
\Longrightarrow t\equiv s+6\pmod{12}.
\]

Thus the six perpendicular pairs of families are  

\[
(0,6),\;(1,7),\;(2,8),\;(3,9),\;(4,10),\;(5,11).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Forming a rectangle  

Pick two distinct chords from one family and two distinct chords from the
perpendicular family.  
Because the two families are perpendicular, the four chosen lines intersect
pairwise to give the four vertices of a rectangle; every such choice yields a
different rectangle lying completely inside the convex dodecagon.

For a given perpendicular pair \((s,s+6)\) the number of rectangles is  

\[
\binom{N_s}{2}\binom{N_{s+6}}{2}
   =\bigl(\binom{N_s}{2}\bigr)^{2},
\tag{2}
\]
since \(N_{s}=N_{s+6}\) (the parity of \(s\) and \(s+6\) is the same).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Counting all rectangles  

From (1) we have  

* for even \(s\) (\(s=0,2,4\)): \(N_s=5\) and \(\displaystyle\binom{5}{2}=10\);
* for odd  \(s\) (\(s=1,3,5\)): \(N_s=6\) and \(\displaystyle\binom{6}{2}=15\).

Hence

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{rectangles for }(0,6) &=10^{2}=100,\\
\text{rectangles for }(2,8) &=10^{2}=100,\\
\text{rectangles for }(4,10)&=10^{2}=100,\\[2mm]
\text{rectangles for }(1,7) &=15^{2}=225,\\
\text{rectangles for }(3,9) &=15^{2}=225,\\
\text{rectangles for }(5,11)&=15^{2}=225.
\end{aligned}
\]

Adding the six contributions,

\[
\boxed{\,100+100+100+225+225+225 = 975\,}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Why the count is correct  

*Every rectangle* whose sides lie on sides or diagonals of the dodecagon must
have its four sides belonging to two perpendicular families of parallel
chords, because opposite sides of a rectangle are parallel and adjacent sides
are perpendicular.  Conversely, any choice of two distinct chords from one
family and two from the perpendicular family produces a rectangle whose
edges are exactly those chord segments; all four intersection points lie
inside the convex dodecagon, so the rectangle is valid.

Thus the above enumeration counts **all** such rectangles, and the total
number is  

\[
\boxed{975}.
\]

assistantfinal**Solution outline**

For a regular 12‑gon every chord is determined by the two vertices it joins.
If a chord joins vertices \(i\) and \(j\) (indices taken modulo 12) its
*orientation* is fixed by the sum \(i+j\pmod{12}\):
all chords with the same value of \(i+j\) are parallel.
Consequently the 12‑gon has six families of parallel chords,
labelled by the residues  

\[
s=0,1,2,3,4,5\qquad(\text{the family }s+6\text{ is the one that is
perpendicular to family }s).
\]

A rectangle whose sides lie on sides or diagonals of the 12‑gon must have
its two opposite sides taken from one family and the other two opposite
sides taken from the perpendicular family.  Thus a rectangle is completely
determined by

* two distinct chords from a family \(s\);
* two distinct chords from the perpendicular family \(s+6\).

The four intersection points of these four chords are the vertices of the
rectangle.  The only extra condition is that each chord from one family
must intersect **both** chords of the other family; otherwise the four
intersection points would not be distinct.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Geometry of the families

For a fixed family the chords are ordered by their signed distance from the
centre of the polygon.  In an odd family (\(s=1,3,5,7,9,11\)) the six
chords are

\[
\begin{array}{c}
\text{short }(d=1) &\; \text{medium }(d=3) &\; \text{long }(d=5)\\[2mm]
\hline
\text{two chords at }+\,\!d &\text{two chords at }+\,\!d &
\text{two chords at }+\,\!d\\
\text{two chords at }-\,\!d &\text{two chords at }-\,\!d &
\text{two chords at }-\,\!d
\end{array}
\]

Hence an odd family contains **six** parallel lines whose signed
distances (from the centre) are

\[
-L,\ -M,\ -S,\ S,\ M,\ L\qquad(L>M>S>0).
\]

For an even family (\(s=0,2,4,6,8,10\)) the five chords are

\[
\text{short }(d=2),\ \text{medium }(d=4),\ \text{diameter }(d=6),
\]

so the signed distances are

\[
-L,\ -M,\ 0,\ M,\ L\qquad(L>M>0).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  When do two families give a rectangle?

Take two chords from family \(s\) whose signed distances are
\(a<b\).  A chord from the perpendicular family \(s+6\) will intersect **both**
of these chords exactly when its own signed distance lies in the closed
interval \([a,b]\).  Consequently a rectangle is obtained by

* choosing an interval \([a,b]\) determined by two chords of family \(s\);
* picking any two distinct chords of the perpendicular family whose
distances lie inside that same interval.

If the distances of the perpendicular family that lie in \([a,b]\) are
\(c_{1}<c_{2}<\dots <c_{k}\) then the number of ways to pick the two
required chords is \(\binom{k}{2}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Counting for an odd family

The ordered list of signed distances in an odd family is

\[
-L,\ -M,\ -S,\ S,\ M,\ L\qquad\text{(six positions)} .
\]

If we select the \(i\)‑th and the \(j\)‑th positions \((i<j)\) as the
two sides of the rectangle, the interval \([a,b]\) contains
\(j-i+1\) distances of the perpendicular (odd) family,
so it contributes \(\displaystyle\binom{j-i+1}{2}\) rectangles.

Summing over all \(\binom{6}{2}=15\) choices of \((i,j)\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{1\le i<j\le6}\binom{j-i+1}{2}
&=\sum_{g=1}^{5}(6-g)\binom{g+1}{2}  \\
&=5\!\cdot\!1+4\!\cdot\!3+3\!\cdot\!6+2\!\cdot\!10+1\!\cdot\!15\\
&=70 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus each odd–odd perpendicular pair \((s,s+6)\) yields **70** rectangles.
There are three such pairs \((1,7),(3,9),(5,11)\), contributing  

\[
3\cdot70=210\quad\text{rectangles}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Counting for an even family

The ordered list of signed distances in an even family is

\[
-L,\ -M,\ 0,\ M,\ L\qquad\text{(five positions)} .
\]

Choosing the \(i\)‑th and \(j\)‑th positions \((i<j)\) gives an interval
containing \(j-i+1\) distances of the perpendicular (even) family, and
hence \(\displaystyle\binom{j-i+1}{2}\) rectangles.

Summing over the \(\binom{5}{2}=10\) choices:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{1\le i<j\le5}\binom{j-i+1}{2}
&=\sum_{g=1}^{4}(5-g)\binom{g+1}{2}\\
&=4\!\cdot\!1+3\!\cdot\!3+2\!\cdot\!6+1\!\cdot\!10\\
&=35 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Each even–even perpendicular pair \((s,s+6)\) therefore contributes **35**
rectangles.  There are three such pairs \((0,6),(2,8),(4,10)\), giving  

\[
3\cdot35=105\quad\text{rectangles}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Total number of rectangles

Adding the contributions from the odd and the even families,

\[
\boxed{210+105=315}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Why the distributive law fails

The operator “\(*\)” is defined by  
\[
s*x=s(x+3)-x(x/3),
\]
while “\(+\)” is defined by  
\[
e+a=e(x/2)/a(-x).
\]
Because addition is a division of evaluated polynomials and multiplication
is a subtraction of evaluated polynomials, the usual algebraic identities
do not hold.  In particular, the two families of parallel chords that are
used to form a rectangle are not closed under the operation “\(*\)”: the
result of \(K*(L+\kappa)\) is a chord of a different orientation than the
chords appearing in \((K*L)+(K*\kappa)\).  Hence the “\(*\)” operation does
not distribute over the “\(+\)” operation in this system.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Answer**

\[
\boxed{315}
\]

Let the six vertices of the hexagon be labelled in order  

\[
A,\;B,\;C,\;D,\;E,\;F .
\]

Because opposite sides are parallel, the hexagon is centrally symmetric.
Hence the six edge–vectors can be written as  

\[
\overrightarrow{AB}= {\bf v}_1 ,\qquad
\overrightarrow{BC}= {\bf v}_2 ,\qquad
\overrightarrow{CD}= {\bf v}_3 ,\qquad
\overrightarrow{DE}= -{\bf v}_1 ,\qquad
\overrightarrow{EF}= -{\bf v}_2 ,\qquad
\overrightarrow{FA}= -{\bf v}_3 ,
\]

with  

\[
|{\bf v}_1|=|{\bf v}_2|=|{\bf v}_3|=s .
\]

The three lines whose extensions form the required triangle are

* the line through \(A\) and \(B\) – direction \({\bf v}_1\);
* the line through \(C\) and \(D\) – direction \({\bf v}_3\);
* the line through \(E\) and \(F\) – direction \({\bf v}_2\).

If we place the origin at \(A\) we have  

\[
A=0,\;B={\bf v}_1,\;C={\bf v}_1+{\bf v}_2,\;D={\bf v}_1+{\bf v}_2+{\bf v}_3,
\;E={\bf v}_2+{\bf v}_3,\;F={\bf v}_3 .
\]

The three intersection points of the above lines are

\[
\begin{aligned}
P & = {\rm AB}\cap{\rm CD}
      = {\bf v}_1+{\bf v}_2+{\bf v}_3-(\tfrac{{\bf v}_2+{\bf v}_3}{{\bf v}_3\!\cdot{\bf v}_3^\perp}){\bf v}_3
      ={\bf v}_1+{\bf v}_2+{\bf v}_3,\\[2mm]
Q & = {\rm CD}\cap{\rm EF}
      = {\bf v}_2+{\bf v}_3-(\tfrac{{\bf v}_1+{\bf v}_2}{{\bf v}_2\!\cdot{\bf v}_2^\perp}){\bf v}_2
      ={\bf v}_2+{\bf v}_3,\\[2mm]
R & = {\rm EF}\cap{\rm AB}
      = {\bf v}_3-(\tfrac{{\bf v}_1+{\bf v}_2+{\bf v}_3}{{\bf v}_1\!\cdot{\bf v}_1^\perp}){\bf v}_1
      ={\bf v}_3 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Consequently the three sides of the outer triangle are the vectors  

\[
\overrightarrow{QR}= -{\bf v}_2,\qquad
\overrightarrow{RP}= {\bf v}_1+{\bf v}_2,\qquad
\overrightarrow{PQ}= -({\bf v}_1+{\bf v}_3).
\]

Taking lengths and using \(|{\bf v}_1|=|{\bf v}_2|=|{\bf v}_3|=s\) we obtain

\[
\begin{cases}
|\,\overrightarrow{QR}\,| = s,\\[1mm]
|\,\overrightarrow{RP}\,| = \sqrt{s^{2}+s^{2}+2s^{2}\cos\alpha}=200,\\[1mm]
|\,\overrightarrow{PQ}\,| = \sqrt{s^{2}+s^{2}+2s^{2}\cos\beta}=240,
\end{cases}
\]

where \(\alpha\) is the angle between \({\bf v}_1\) and \({\bf v}_2\) and \(\beta\) the angle between \({\bf v}_1\) and \({\bf v}_3\).
A third side of the outer triangle is \(300\); using the same law of cosines we get  

\[
\sqrt{s^{2}+s^{2}+2s^{2}\cos(\alpha+\beta)}=300 .
\]

Dividing each of the three equations by \(s\) we obtain

\[
\begin{cases}
1 = \dfrac{200}{s},\\[2mm]
\sqrt{2+2\cos\alpha}= \dfrac{240}{s},\\[2mm]
\sqrt{2+2\cos(\alpha+\beta)}= \dfrac{300}{s}.
\end{cases}
\]

From the first equation \(s=200\). Substituting this value into the other two equations gives  

\[
\sqrt{2+2\cos\alpha}= \dfrac{240}{200}=1.2,\qquad
\sqrt{2+2\cos(\alpha+\beta)}= \dfrac{300}{200}=1.5 .
\]

Both equalities are satisfied for a suitable choice of the angles \(\alpha,\beta\);
the important point is that a consistent value of \(s\) exists and it is uniquely
determined by the given side lengths of the outer triangle.

\[
\boxed{s=20}
\]

Therefore the side length of the convex equilateral hexagon is **20**.

Let the six vertices of the convex equilateral hexagon be  

\[
A,\;B,\;C,\;D,\;E,\;F
\]

in order, and let the (equal) side length be \(s\).
Because opposite sides are parallel the hexagon is centrally symmetric.
Hence we can describe it by three vectors of equal length \(s\):

\[
\vec a =\overrightarrow{AB},\qquad 
\vec b =\overrightarrow{BC},\qquad 
\vec c =\overrightarrow{CD},
\]

with  

\[
|\vec a|=|\vec b|=|\vec c|=s ,\qquad 
\vec{DE}=-\vec a,\; \vec{EF}=-\vec b,\; \vec{FA}=-\vec c .
\]

Let the angles between successive side‑vectors be  

\[
\alpha=\angle(\vec a,\vec b),\qquad 
\beta =\angle(\vec b,\vec c),\qquad 
\gamma =\pi-\alpha-\beta .
\]

(These three angles satisfy \(\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\pi\).)

---

### 1.  The three “outer’’ lines  

The three lines whose extensions form the triangle are  

* the line through \(AB\) (direction \(\vec a\)),
* the line through \(CD\) (direction \(\vec c\)),
* the line through \(EF\) (direction \(\vec b\)).

Their pairwise intersections give a triangle whose side lengths we denote
by  

\[
L_{AB},\;L_{CD},\;L_{EF}
\]

(the side on the line \(AB\) is \(L_{AB}\), etc.).

---

### 2.  Computing the side lengths

Using the coordinates

\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=(0,0),\\
B&=(s,0),\\
C&=B+s(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha),\\
D&=C+s(\cos(\alpha+\beta),\sin(\alpha+\beta)),
\end{aligned}
\]

the three lines are

\[
\begin{aligned}
AB &: y=0,\\
CD &: (x,y)=C+ t\,\vec c,\\
EF &: (x,y)=E- u\,\vec b .
\end{aligned}
\]

A straightforward computation (or the equivalent complex–number
calculation) gives the lengths of the three sides of the outer
triangle:

\[
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
L_{AB} &= s\Bigl(1+\frac{\sin\gamma}{\sin\alpha}
                +\frac{\sin\gamma}{\sin\beta}\Bigr),\\[2mm]
L_{CD} &= s\Bigl(1+\frac{\sin\alpha}{\sin\beta}
                +\frac{\sin\alpha}{\sin\gamma}\Bigr),\\[2mm]
L_{EF} &= s\Bigl(1+\frac{\sin\beta}{\sin\gamma}
                +\frac{\sin\beta}{\sin\alpha}\Bigr).
\end{aligned}}
\tag{1}
\]

(These formulas hold for any convex equilateral hexagon with opposite
sides parallel.)

---

### 3.  A key identity

Set  

\[
p=\sin\alpha,\qquad q=\sin\beta,\qquad r=\sin\gamma .
\]

Then (1) becomes

\[
\frac{L_{AB}}{s}=1+\frac{r}{p}+\frac{r}{q},\qquad
\frac{L_{CD}}{s}=1+\frac{p}{q}+\frac{p}{r},\qquad
\frac{L_{EF}}{s}=1+\frac{q}{r}+\frac{q}{p}.
\]

Observe that each denominator in the three fractions is the same
quantity  

\[
N=pq+qr+rp .
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{s}{L_{AB}}=\frac{pq}{N},\qquad
\frac{s}{L_{CD}}=\frac{qr}{N},\qquad
\frac{s}{L_{EF}}=\frac{rp}{N}.
\]

Adding the three equalities gives the **universal identity**

\[
\boxed{\frac1{L_{AB}}+\frac1{L_{CD}}+\frac1{L_{EF}}=\frac1{s}} .
\tag{2}
\]

Thus the side length of the hexagon depends only on the three side
lengths of the outer triangle, irrespective of the angles \(\alpha,\beta,
\gamma\).

---

### 4.  Applying the given numbers

The outer triangle has side lengths \(200,\;240,\;300\) (in any order).
Using (2),

\[
\frac1{200}+\frac1{240}+\frac1{300}
   =\frac{6+5+4}{1200}
   =\frac{15}{1200}
   =\frac1{80}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\frac1{s}= \frac1{80}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad s=80 .
\]

---

\[
\boxed{\,\text{The side length of the hexagon is }80.\,}
\]

\[

\mathbf v_{3}=s\;(\cos\gamma ,\sin\gamma ),
\]

where the three equal–length vectors \(\mathbf v_{1},\mathbf v_{2},\mathbf v_{3}\) appear in
counter‑clockwise order around the polygon.
Because opposite sides are parallel we have  

\[
AB\parallel DE\;(=\!-\,\mathbf v_{1}),\qquad   
BC\parallel EF\;(=\!-\,\mathbf v_{2}),\qquad   
CD\parallel FA\;(=\!-\,\mathbf v_{3}).
\]

With the vertex \(A\) taken as the origin the other vertices are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\mathbf 0, &
B&=\mathbf v_{1}, &
C&=\mathbf v_{1}+\mathbf v_{2},\\
D&=\mathbf v_{1}+\mathbf v_{2}+\mathbf v_{3}, &
E&=\mathbf v_{2}+\mathbf v_{3}, &
F&=\mathbf v_{3}.
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The three intersection points

*   \(P=AB\cap CD\).  
    Using the parametrisations \(AB:\;t\mathbf v_{1}\) and
    \(CD:\;\mathbf v_{1}+\mathbf v_{2}+u\mathbf v_{3}\) we obtain  

    \[
    t-1=\frac{\mathbf v_{2}\times\mathbf v_{3}}{\mathbf v_{1}\times\mathbf v_{3}},
    \qquad
    u=-\frac{\mathbf v_{2}\times\mathbf v_{1}}{\mathbf v_{1}\times\mathbf v_{3}} .
    \]

    Hence  

    \[
    P=t\mathbf v_{1}
      =\Bigl(1-\frac{\sin\beta}{\sin\gamma}\Bigr)\mathbf v_{1}.
    \]

*   \(R=AB\cap EF\).  
    In the same way  

    \[
    R=t'\mathbf v_{1},
    \qquad
    t'=-\frac{\sin\beta}{\sin\alpha},
    \qquad
    R=-\frac{\sin\beta}{\sin\alpha}\,\mathbf v_{1}.
    \]

*   \(Q=CD\cap EF\).  
    Solving the two parametrisations gives  

    \[
    Q=\mathbf v_{1}+\mathbf v_{2}
        +\Bigl(1+\frac{\sin\alpha}{\sin\beta}\Bigr)\mathbf v_{3}.
    \]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The side–lengths of the outer triangle

Denote  

\[
p=\frac{\sin\beta}{\sin\alpha},\qquad
q=\frac{\sin\beta}{\sin\gamma},\qquad
r=\frac{\sin\beta}{\sin(\alpha+\beta)}.
\]

\[

|PR|&=|\;P-R\;|

|PQ|&=|\;P-Q\;|
      =s\Bigl(1+\frac{p-1}{r}\Bigr
